FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Describe the epidemiology, etiology, and natural history of metastatic carcinoma to bone.
Apply scoring systems to estimate the risk of pathologic fracture in patients with metastatic
bone lesions.
Determine the components of a comprehensive evaluation of an osteolytic bone lesion in a
patient with no known primary malignancy.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Metastasis, derived from an ancient Greek word methistanai, meaning “to change the setting,”
was used by Joseph Récamier in 1829 to describe the process of tumor dissemination to other



organs. Metastasis to bone was later described by Stephen Paget, who analyzed autopsy
specimens of women who died of metastatic breast cancer.
Metastatic bone disease often presents as pain, hypercalcemia, pathologic fracture, nerve
compression, or pancytopenia from marrow invasion.
Because pain is a common presenting symptom in patients with metastatic bone disease,
orthopaedic surgeons, regardless of subspecialty, will aid in the multidisciplinary treatment of
these patients.
Orthopaedic surgeons must have a thorough understanding of the pathophysiology and
behavior of bone metastasis to guide the initial evaluation and management of this disease.
Epidemiology
Metastatic bone disease is most common in patients older than 40 years. Metastatic
carcinoma is the most common reason for an osteolytic bone lesion in this age group. Among
the more than 1.73 million cases of cancer per year in the United States, bone metastasis will
be present in approximately 50% at some point in the disease course.1
As systematic treatment options improve, patients with metastatic cancer are living longer;
therefore, the prevalence of metastatic bone disease is expected to increase.
Sites of metastasis
Bone is the third most common site for carcinoma to metastasize, behind the lungs and
liver.2
Primary cancer types (Resource 1)
Although all tumors are capable of metastasizing to bone, the most common primary
cancers that do so are breast, prostate, lung, kidney, and thyroid (in order of most to least
common). Breast and prostate cancer represent approximately 80% of bone metastases.3
Economic effects of bony metastasis
Metastatic bone disease is a considerable driver of the economic burden of cancer, with
mean direct medical costs of $75,329 to care for a patient with metastatic bone disease
versus $31,382 for control patients without bony involvement. The national cost burden for
the subset of cancer with metastatic bone disease was estimated at $12.6 billion per year,
which represents 17% of the $74 billion in total direct medical costs for cancer estimated by
the National Institutes of Health in 2004).4
Anatomy and Biomechanics

Anatomy
The most common sites for skeletal metastasis include the spine, pelvis, ribs, and proximal
extremities (proximal femur and humerus).3
The location of bony metastasis can be explained by the presence of the Batson venous
plexus, which is a valveless plexus of veins around the spine that allows tumor cells to travel to
the vertebral bodies, pelvis, ribs, skull, and proximal limb girdle (Figure 1). This phenomenon
is commonly described in patients with prostate cancer.
Figure 1
Illustration shows the structure of the Batson venous plexus around the spine, which accounts
for the propensity of metastases from carcinoma to settle in the axial skeleton. (Reproduced
with permission from Carpenter K, Decater T, Iwanaga J, et al: Revisiting the vertebral venous
plexus: A comprehensive review of the literature. World Neurosurg 2021;145:381-395.)
Acral (distal to the elbow or knee) metastases are commonly related to lung or renal
carcinoma (Figures 2 and 3).

Biomechanics
If metastatic disease results in cortical destruction, the destroyed portion of cortical bone
results in structural weakness. The size and number of lesions, their locations, and the
structural importance of the missing bone contribute to the risk of pathologic fracture.

Biomechanical principles may be useful in predicting the risk of pathologic fracture in a clinical
setting.
Finite element analysis studies have identified the inferomedial femoral neck and the
anterolateral proximal femur at the level of the lesser trochanter as the locations at which
lytic lesions portend the most risk of pathologic fracture.5
In the future, CT-based algorithms may play a larger role in predicting the risk of pathologic
fracture.6
Etiology
Two primary hypotheses exist with regard to why certain carcinomas favor metastatic spread
to certain sites of bone.
Seed and soil
In 1889, Stephen Paget described a seed and soil hypothesis, which stated that certain
tumor cells are able to survive and grow in compatible end-organ environments that have
the optimal concentration of oxygen and other nutritional factors. This may explain why
certain types of carcinoma have predilection for bone.7
This is supported by studies demonstrating that disseminated tumor cells exist throughout
the circulation and other organs in the body; however, only 0.01% of these
micrometastases survive, suggesting that successful metastatic progression requires an
interaction between the tumor cells and the local environment.
Circulation theory
In 1928, James Ewing described a competing circulation theory, which stated that the
location of metastasis is dictated primarily by the geography of where circulation takes
tumor cells. In this theory, organs are passive receptacles, and tumor cells tend to migrate
to the location circulation takes them first.8
The existence of the Batson plexus—a venous plexus around the spine that feeds the
vertebral bodies, pelvis, ribs, skull, and proximal limb girdle—is the classic example
supporting this theory.9
Pathophysiology/molecular mechanisms
Stepwise progression to metastasis
Mechanism for bone destruction is mediated via the receptor activator of nuclear factor-
factor-kappa B ligand (RANKL) pathway (Figure 5).

Disease-specific factors
Breast cancer
Other disease-specific factors
Prostate cancer
Endothelin 1 expressed by prostate cancer cells stimulates osteoblasts to produce bone,
explaining the typical osteoblastic appearance of metastatic prostate cancer.
Renal cell carcinoma
Overexpression of growth factors and receptors related to vascular proliferation is
common in renal cell carcinoma.
These include epidermal growth factor receptor, vascular endothelial growth factor
receptor, and platelet-derived growth factor receptor.13

This fact likely explains the propensity for metastases of renal cell carcinoma to be highly
vascularized, which may lead to high blood loss during management of these metastases if
unprepared. Thyroid carcinoma and myeloma can similarly be associated with high blood
loss.
Therefore, renal cell carcinomas may benefit from embolization before surgical resection or
stabilization.14
Embolization is recommended for procedures in which a lesion will be entered.
Embolization may not be necessary in lesions amenable to tourniquet control and/or
wide resection.
Wide resection of metastatic disease may be associated with improved survival duration in
oligometastatic renal cell carcinoma15 (Figure 7).
Figure 7

carcinoma unless a tourniquet can be used during surgical treatment. C, AP radiograph

Fracture healing in pathologic bone
The likelihood of healing after pathologic fracture also seems to be dependent on the
underlying disease process, with bony healing more likely in patients with multiple
myeloma (67%) than in patients with renal (44%), breast (37%), or lung (zero) carcinoma.16
Other physiologic disruptions
Calcium homeostasis
Hypercalcemia is the most common metabolic derangement observed in cancer patients
and is present in 10% to 30% of patients.
Calcium abnormalities are especially common with lung and breast cancer metastasis.
The degree of calcium derangement does not correlate with the number of bone
metastases or whether the disease process is osteolytic or osteoblastic.
Early symptoms of hypercalcemia include polyuria/polydipsia, anorexia, weakness, easy
fatigability, dehydration, and constipation.
Late symptoms of hypercalcemia include irritability, depression, coma, profound
weakness, nausea/vomiting, pruritus, and vision abnormalities.
Management requires aggressive hydration to prevent renal complications and
intravenous bisphosphonate therapy to help reduce serum calcium levels.
Hematopoiesis
Normocytic/normochromic anemia is common with breast, prostate, lung, and thyroid
cancer metastasis, as the bone marrow becomes displaced by metastatic disease.
Clotting cascade
In general, patients with malignancy have an increased risk of thromboembolic events.
Mechanical and chemoprophylaxis usually is indicated in these patients, especially those
who are undergoing lower extremity/pelvic surgery.
Tumor cells activate thrombin and fibrin formation directly via release of procoagulants.
Tumor cells activate thrombin and fibrin formation indirectly via the activation of
endothelial cells, leukocytes, and platelets by cytokines.
Pain control
The pain associated with cancer often may be difficult to control. Usually a multimodal
regimen via a combination of narcotic and nonnarcotic medications is indicated, and
consultation with pain services often may be helpful.
Care also must be taken to mitigate the adverse effects of pain medication, including
severe constipation associated with narcotic agents and upper gastrointestinal issues
associated with NSAIDs.

Etiology
Primary tumor cells grow via unchecked cell proliferation and stimulation of local
angiogenesis to support the growing primary mass. A subset of the tumor cells will
eventually develop the ability to evade host defenses, cross the capillary basement
membrane, and enter the bloodstream. The tumor cells then disseminate to distant
sites and come to rest in a distant capillary bed. This is accomplished via the use of
integrins, cadherins, and matrix metalloproteinases, which allow tumor cells to
adhere to the vascular endothelium and extravasate into the end-organ environment.
Tumor cells then interact with host cells at the metastatic site and proliferate there to
form a metastatic mass with the help of growth factors (transforming growth factor-
beta [TGF-ß], insulin-like growth factor, fibroblast growth factor, bone morphogenetic
protein).
Tumor cells do not directly destroy bone; rather, they express cytokines that influence
the bone turnover process. Tumor cells stimulate the secretion of RANKL via
osteoblasts, which causes an increase in osteoclast precursors and eventually results
in increased osteoclastic bone resorption.
The RANKL pathway is a critical therapeutic target in managing metastatic bone
disease, and diphosphonates and denosumab (an anti-RANKL monoclonal antibody)
have been found to delay time to skeletal-related events, such as pathologic fracture,
spinal cord compression, and/or the need for radiation therapy/surgery.10-12
TGF-ß, which normally is stored in the bone and released during normal bone
turnover, will stimulate breast cancer cells to secrete parathyroid hormone-related
protein. Parathyroid hormone-related protein from cancer cells is a potent activator
of the RANKL pathway, in which RANKL from osteoblasts stimulates osteoclast
precursors and increases osteoclasts. Osteoclasts destroy bone, which releases more
TGF-ß, and the cycle of destruction repeats (Figure 6). Breast cancer cells also secrete
osteoclastic stimulants (interleukin 6, interleukin 8), which directly increases
osteoclastic activity.

Figure 6

differentiate in response to metastasis-derived signals mediated by parathyroid
hormone-related protein (PTHrP). The osteoblasts are stimulated and release
macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF) and receptor activator or nuclear
factor-kappa B ligand (RANKL), leading to increased osteoclast production and
maturation. Mature osteoclasts secrete acidophilic proteases that mediate bone
reabsorption. The release of TGF-ß stimulates the production of PTHrP, thus
completing the cycle. IGF = insulin-like growth factor, IL = interleukin, OPG =
osteoprotegerin. (Adapted with permission from Buijs JT, van der Pluijm G:
Osteotropic cancers: From primary tumor to bone. Cancer Lett 2009;273[2]:177-193.)

Natural History
At time of death, 70% of patients with prostate or breast carcinoma have bone metastases.17
Survival
Being able to predict the remaining lifespan of patients with metastatic carcinoma has been
an area of considerable interest.
Multiple prognostic models exist for patients with bone metastases from carcinoma, such as
the PATHFx clinical decision support tool (Resource 2), which may aid in decision making
regarding appropriate management.18-21
These models typically identify the following as considerable prognostic factors: presence
of visceral metastasis, multiple metastases, pathologic fracture, and type of primary tumor
involved.22,23
Pathologic fractures
Reducing the probability of pathologic fractures resulting from metastatic bone disease is of
paramount concern for orthopaedic oncologists. Patients who require stabilization after
having sustained a pathologic fracture have worse pain, diminished functional outcomes,
and inferior oncologic outcomes compared with patients who undergo prophylactic fixation
before impending pathologic fracture.24
Analyses also have demonstrated that patients who undergo prophylactic stabilization have
a lower risk of 30-day major postoperative complications and shorter hospital length of stay
compared with patients requiring treatment after a fracture.25
Other investigators have demonstrated a survival benefit from prophylactic fixation
compared to internal fixation of a completed fracture.26
The direct costs associated with management of an acute pathologic fracture are
considerably higher than with successful prophylactic fixation.27
Classification of Risk Factors
Numerous classification systems have been proposed that attempt to estimate the risk of
impending pathologic fracture and guide management.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Orthopaedic surgeons will encounter patients with metastatic bone disease. The ability to
recognize this entity, perform an initial evaluation, and appropriately treat or refer these

evaluation and diagnosis of bony metastasis has been studied at length, and an algorithm for
the workup of patients older than 40 years with a destructive bone lesion has been
developed28 (Table 1).

Patient History
Patients typically present with symptoms of progressive pain that are worse with weight
bearing (functional pain).
Bone cancer pain may begin as intermittent pain but often becomes more constant and less
controlled with increasing doses of analgesic agents.
Pain from metastatic bone disease may result from mechanical causes, such as increased
intraosseous pressure, periosteal distention, perineural invasion, and impending or completed

9/3/26, 5:34 PM
AAOS | Pathophysiology of Bone Metastasis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001165
14/27

pathologic fractures. This pain often can be considerably improved via skeletal stabilization,
radiation therapy, and/or ablative procedures.29-31
Asking about a personal or family history of cancer is imperative, with the knowledge that
primary cancers may occasionally metastasize quickly; however, patients may have been living
with a cancer diagnosis for 10 to 15 years before metastasis occurs (particularly in those with
breast, renal, or prostate cancer). If the patient does not have a known primary site of cancer,
a careful review of systems must be performed, with particular attention paid to the organ
systems related to the cancers that commonly metastasize to bone: lumps/masses, cough,
chest pain, shortness of breath, hot/cold intolerance, hair loss, unintentional weight gain/loss,
nausea/vomiting, abdominal distention, early satiety, changes in bowel/bladder function,
difficulty urinating, and hematuria.
Physical Examination
Note whether a patient has pain with weight bearing; substantial pain with gait or weight
bearing is a symptom concerning for impending pathologic fracture. Patients may exhibit a
limp because of an antalgic gait, guarding of the affected limb, or decreased range of motion.
If a patient is nonambulatory, a straight leg raise against gravity is another useful test of the
integrity of the peritrochanteric region. This maneuver places stress more than twice a
patient’s body weight across the hip joint, and the absence of pain with this maneuver is
relatively reassuring against an impending pathologic fracture.32
Other findings that may be obtained via physical examination include swelling or neurologic
deficits at sites of metastatic bone disease.
Regional lymphadenopathy is common with metastatic bone disease, and a lymph node
examination should be performed in the affected limb.
Depending on the site of primary cancer, breast, prostate, thyroid, and abdominal masses may
be palpable on physical examination.
Diagnostic Modalities
Radiography
Evaluation
Radiographs always should include the entire bone affected and at least two orthogonal
planes.
Appearance

Osteolytic
Metastases from lung, thyroid, renal, and gastrointestinal malignancies tend appear be
radiolucent on radiographs, indicating an osteolytic process.
Osteoblastic
Prostate and bladder cancers classically have a calcified matrix that appears radiolucent on
radiographs, indicating an osteoblastic process (Figure 8).
Figure 8
Radiographs show osteolytic and osteoblastic metastases. A, AP radiograph of a left hip
demonstrates lung cancer metastases, which generally are purely osteolytic. Note the
lesion on the left proximal femur that is destroying the lateral cortex. B, AP pelvic
radiograph demonstrates prostate cancer metastases, which are osteoblastic, as noted
throughout the pelvis, spine, and proximal femurs. (Reproduced from Weber KL: Metastatic
bone disease, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1628-1642.)
Mixed osteolytic/osteoblastic
Breast cancers may have a variable radiographic appearance that is intermediate between
the classically osteolytic and osteoblastic types.
Pathologic fracture is common in patients with bony metastasis and more commonly occurs
with osteolytic lesions rather than osteoblastic lesions.
An avulsion of the lesser trochanter implies a pathologic process in the femoral neck/calcar
and an impending pathologic fracture of the proximal femur.
Location

The most common anatomic locations for bony metastasis include the spine (40%), pelvis,
proximal long bones, and ribs.
Spine metastases are most commonly located in the thoracic spine and spare the
intervertebral disk.
Lesions in the extremities tend to occur in the proximal aspects of the upper and lower
extremities.
If metastatic carcinomas appear distal to the elbow or knee, lung cancer most often is the
primary site.
Computed Tomography
CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis
Because some of the most common sites of metastatic disease to the bone in adults are
primarily within the chest (lung, breast), abdominal area (renal/gastrointestinal), and pelvis
(prostate), a CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis often will identify the primary site of
disease in patients with metastatic carcinoma to bone.33
Laboratory Studies
Laboratory studies may be helpful in identifying not only potential primary carcinoma sites but
also other etiologies for bony lesions.
Complete blood count with differential
Anemia may be suggestive of myeloma or extensive marrow replacement from any
metastatic process.
Atypical differential on hematology may be suggestive of leukemia, lymphoma, or other
hematologic dyscrasias.
Basic metabolic panel and alkaline phosphatase level, lactate dehydrogenase level
Calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, and lactate dehydrogenase levels are not only
be effective in suggesting a primary metabolic process to explain bony disease but also
may aid in determining the prognosis and treatment response of primary bone tumors and
metastatic disease.34,35
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level
These laboratory tests may be helpful in the diagnosis of osteomyelitis.
Thyroid studies

A basic thyroid panel, including thyroid-stimulating hormone and free T4 index is effective
at detecting most forms of thyroid cancer.
Urinalysis
Microscopic hematuria is one of the signs of renal cell or urothelial carcinoma.
Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) and urine protein electrophoresis (UPEP)
SPEP and UPEP are a highly sensitive and specific combination of tests for the detection of
multiple myeloma.
SPEP, along with serum immunofixation, will provide a quantitative level of M-protein and
determine whether the disease is monoclonal or polyclonal with a sensitivity of
approximately 80%.
UPEP allows for detection of kappa or lambda light chain secretion only, which may not be
detected via SPEP alone. The addition of UPEP increases sensitivity to greater than 95%.
SPEP alone is associated with a high negative predictive value, which may make it useful in
ruling out the disease; however, it is most useful in combination with UPEP and/or
biopsy.36
Specific tumor markers
Although the routine use of these markers in the workup of bony metastasis is
controversial, many centers use these markers to find a primary site and/or monitor the
response to systemic therapy.
Prostate-specific antigen (prostate)
Carcinoembryonic antigen (colon, pancreas)
Cancer antigen 125 (ovarian)
Biopsy
Biopsy of a destructive bone lesion must be performed unless the diagnosis is certain.
Even if a patient has a history of prior carcinoma, surgeons cannot assume that a bony lesion
represents the first instance of metastatic disease. In as many as 15% of patients, a new bony
lesion with known localized carcinoma is found to be a new tumor rather than the first
presentation of metastatic carcinoma. This most frequently occurs in patients with breast
and prostate cancer.37
Placement of an intramedullary device in a patient with a lytic lesion in the femur or sending
reamings for pathology after such a procedure without appropriate prior workup is not
recommended.

Open incisional biopsy or closed needle biopsy (fine-needle aspiration/core) can be performed
before surgical stabilization, usually in the same anesthesia setting.
Overall Diagnostic Strategy
Patient history and physical examination, laboratory studies, CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis, and
biopsy
If using this diagnostic algorithm, the primary site of disease can be localized in 85% of
patients.38
15% of osteolytic skeletal lesions remain undiagnosed.
Poorer overall prognosis
Next steps may include panendoscopy of the ears/nose/throat to evaluate for possible
head/neck neoplasm, esophagogastroduodenoscopy, colonoscopy, and mammography.
Positron emission tomography/CT is an additional consideration but has been shown to
result in low diagnostic yield in identification of the primary malignancy in this setting.38
Supplemental Diagnostic Modalities
Bone Scintigraphy
Although bone scintigraphy is not useful in finding the primary site of disease, it is
recommended as part of the evaluation of an adult patient with bony disease.
Bone scintigraphy is most useful in its ability to detect osteoblastic activity (may be negative in
myeloma and metastatic renal cancer).
Multiple sites of metastasis are common, and bone scintigraphy is a relatively inexpensive and
effective way to assess the overall burden of disease and locate lesions that may have
consequences in terms of impending fracture or considerations for surgical anesthesia (eg,
cervical spine disease, which would necessitate advanced intubation techniques).
In evaluating a patient with a new diagnosis, bone scintigraphy may identify a more accessible
lesion for biopsy.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI of the primary lesion generally is not necessary unless defining disease in the spine or
attempting to determine marrow or soft-tissue extent if it will affect the surgical treatment
plan (Figure 9).

Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography occasionally may be used as an adjunct to diagnosis and/or staging to assess
soft-tissue masses or lymph nodes.
Positron Emission Tomography
Recently, positron emission tomography has been studied as a possible adjunct or
replacement to traditional staging studies.
However, recent studies suggest that, although positron emission tomography/CT may be
useful in assessing overall metastatic burden, it does not outperform a standard evaluation for
the identification of primary cancer in patients with a skeletal metastasis of unknown primary
origin.38

Bone Marrow Biopsy
Bone marrow biopsy may be appropriate if myeloma is being considered as a diagnosis.
Pathology
Histologic appearance of metastatic carcinoma is similar to the tissue of origin.
The typical histologic appearance of metastatic carcinoma is described as islands of epithelial
cells, with glandular or squamous differentiation.
Depending on the histology of the primary tumor site, the glandular structures may be
clearly visible within the metastatic tumor. These cells often have tight junctions between
them and reside in a fibrous stroma, which is reasonable given the natural function of these
cells.
Disease-specific features on histology
Follicular subtypes of thyroid carcinoma may exhibit a distinctive appearance of follicles filled
with colloid material.
Clear cell subtypes of renal cell carcinoma may have cells with a clear appearance to the
cytoplasm, whereas other forms of renal cell may be poorly differentiated or sarcomatous-
appearing (Figure 10).

Kidney: CD10, vimentin, PAX8
Differential Diagnosis
Differential diagnosis of a lytic bone lesion in patients older than 40 years includes metastatic
disease, multiple myeloma, and lymphoma. Less likely diagnoses include primary bone
tumors, hyperparathyroidism (brown tumor), and osteomyelitis.
Differentiating osteoporosis from metastatic disease is difficult in patients with a single
vertebral compression fracture. Soft-tissue mass and pedicle destruction (the winking owl sign)
are suggestive of metastatic cancer as an etiology.
Conclusion
Bony metastasis from carcinoma is common in adults older than 40 years, and pathologic
fracture from bony metastases may be a debilitating complication.
Knowledge of the pathophysiology of bone metastasis allows orthopaedic surgeons to
systematically diagnose bony lesions and identify their primary sites, assess the risk of
pathologic fracture, and make correct decisions regarding treatment to substantially improve
patient survival and function.
